title: What They Remembered
subtitle: Past-Life Sessions, Honestly Told
description_paragraphs: She described the staircase before I asked about the house. She counted forty-one steps, and then she said "forty-one, always forty-one" in a voice that was not the voice she had been using with me.

That is the kind of moment this book is full of, and it is also the kind of moment that usually gets written up as something it is not. A regression session is testimony: an accurate record of what a person said and felt in a chair, and not a record of the world outside it. A great many accounts in this genre slide from the first to the second somewhere around the verbs, and readers who go and check one claim tend not to come back.

What They Remembered follows nine sessions, in eight chapters, from the chair to the check — the words, the silences, the crying, the two minutes a man could not speak. The sessions are composite accounts, written from the way sessions of this kind actually go, and nobody in them is a real, identifiable client; the book says so on its first page. Wherever a session touches something that could be looked up, the book shows what checking it involves and what such checks honestly return. Most of the time that is nothing, and the book says nothing, in that word. The one apparent match is taken apart in the chapter that reports it.
It is not a debunking. It takes the chair seriously and it takes you seriously enough not to dress a session up as proof.

A woman counts forty-one stairs out loud and says "always forty-one" in a voice that is not hers. A man who has avoided open water for twenty years describes a wet rope and cannot speak for two minutes. A woman repeats a name she cannot pronounce, and nothing anywhere answers to it — which the book reports as nothing, because that is what it is. Another session goes nowhere at all: an hour of a man lying quietly, reporting the colour behind his eyelids. It is in here too, because eight session chapters with no empty ones would be telling you something false about what a session is. What people say changed for them afterwards is reported as what they said, and no more: nothing here promises that anything will change for you.

Along the way: what the hour before a session decides, and why it matters more than the induction. The six words that smuggle a claim, and the plainer ones that do not. The question a practitioner should never ask, and the sessions that taught that lesson the hard way. What the documentary record can and cannot settle, and the arithmetic that quietly dissolves most apparent matches. And the ordinary explanations — forgotten sources, suggestion, the mind's talent for narrative — laid out at full strength rather than waved at, because a reader who has not met them cannot judge anything else in here.

author_bio: Thea Bramwell is a pen name. The sessions in this book are composite accounts, not records of real clients, and the voice that tells them is composed too — the book says so on its first page, at length, rather than in small type at the back. It was written for readers who are drawn to this work and who have stopped trusting the shelf it sits on.
back_cover:
She described the staircase before I asked about the house.

This book follows nine sessions from the chair to the check: the words, the pauses, the crying, the things that come out in a voice the person does not use. They are composite accounts, written from the way such sessions go, and nobody in them is a real, identifiable client. Wherever a session touches something that could be looked up — a name, a date, a place, an object — the book shows what checking it involves and what such checks honestly return, including the times they come back empty.

What it will not do is dress a session up as proof. A regression is testimony, not history, and the difference is the whole book. You will finish it knowing what happens minute by minute in a session, what a practitioner should refuse to promise you, how to prepare for your own, and how to read every other account on this shelf without either swallowing it whole or throwing it out.
